title: Kanishka's council
hookLine: the Kushan king's council in Kashmir, in the northern accounts

lines: COPPER SHEETS, SEALED IN A STUPA.
cards: Sheets of copper, engraved line after line with commentary on the teaching, sealed inside a stupa so the words would last. That is the story the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang recorded about Kashmir.
A few days ago, the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka remembered a council under Ashoka, and a canon written on palm leaves.
Travel north, into Kashmir and beyond, and the accounts kept there remember another gathering, under another king: Kanishka, a ruler of the Kushan empire.

teach.h: A KING TROUBLED BY MANY EXPLANATIONS.
teach.b: First, the king. In the northern accounts, Kanishka is a powerful ruler who becomes a patron of the teaching.
Tradition says he was troubled because the monks he consulted gave him different explanations of the same teachings, and he wanted to know which were sound. Second, the gathering.

So, the accounts say, he called learned monks together in Kashmir. Some name a monk called Vasumitra as its leader, and some link the poet Ashvaghosha with it too. Others place the meeting somewhere else.
The stories agree on the king and the purpose more than on the details. Third, the work. In these accounts the monks didn't write a new canon.
They wrote commentaries: long explanations of the teaching and of the finer points of the Abhidharma, the systematic analysis of mind and experience.

teach.h: COMMENTARIES, SAID TO BE SEALED IN A STUPA.
teach.b: That's where the copper sheets come in: Xuanzang recorded a tradition that these commentaries were engraved on them and sealed inside a stupa. Fourth, why it matters that the accounts differ.
The Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka don't include this council in their list.

teach.h: NORTH AND SOUTH REMEMBER DIFFERENT COUNCILS.
teach.b: The northern schools, and the Tibetan and Chinese histories that drew on them, remember it. Nobody has to decide here which list is right.
Buddhism was already more than one living tradition, with more than one memory of its own past. Each community kept the councils that shaped its own texts.
Hearing the northern account doesn't cancel the southern one. It's another community, telling the story the way it was told to them.

how: Northern Buddhist traditions, including Tibetan and Chinese histories, remember a council under King Kanishka, while the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka count their councils differently; each tradition keeps its own list.

games.q: you're the king. the monks you ask give you different explanations of the same teachings. what do you do?
o: pick the teacher you like best and ignore the rest.
call learned monks together to set out the teaching.
games.why: in the northern accounts, he gathers learned monks in Kashmir, and they compose commentaries on the teaching.

practice: Bring to mind something told or done one way where you grew up and another way somewhere else: a holiday, a recipe, a saint's story, the name for a meal.
Let both versions sit side by side without choosing a winner, noticing what each place keeps and what it leaves out, then come back to the breath, which needs no version at all.
